title: What is a queue — a line where you add at the BACK and remove from the FRONT (First In First Out — FIFO), like a queue at a ticket counter.

s1_definition.profdef: A queue is a linear data structure that follows the First In First Out (FIFO) principle. Elements are added at one end called the rear (or back) and removed from the other end called the front. The two core operations are enqueue, which inserts at the rear, and dequeue, which removes from the front. A queue guarantees that the element waiting the longest is served first.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a line at the National Bank of India cash counter. Rajesh walks in first and stands at the counter. Then Priya arrives and stands behind him. When the teller is ready, Rajesh (who came first) is served first and leaves from the front. Priya moves up. Nobody can jump the line — whoever joined earliest at the back gets served earliest at the front. That orderly line is exactly a queue.
s1_definition.oneliner: A queue is a fair waiting line where the first one in is the first one out.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A queue is a linear data structure that follows the First In First Out (FIFO) principle. Elements are added at one end called the rear (or back) and removed from the other end called the front. The two core operations are enqueue, which inserts at the rear, and dequeue, which removes from the front. A queue guarantees that the element waiting the longest is served first.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine a line at the National Bank of India cash counter. Rajesh walks in first and stands at the counter. Then Priya arrives and stands behind him. When the teller is ready, Rajesh (who came first) is served first and leaves from the front. Priya moves up. Nobody can jump the line — whoever joined earliest at the back gets served earliest at the front. That orderly line is exactly a queue.

**One line to remember:** A queue is a fair waiting line where the first one in is the first one out.

sections.s2_technical:
A queue restricts how you touch the data. You cannot pick an element from the middle. You only add at the rear and remove from the front. This is what makes it predictable and fair.

The main operations are `enqueue`, `dequeue`, `peek`, and `isEmpty`. The `enqueue` operation adds an element at the rear. For example, when a new fund transfer request arrives, we write `pendingTransfers.enqueue(transferRequest)` which places it at the end of the line. The `dequeue` operation removes and returns the element at the front, so `Transfer next = pendingTransfers.dequeue()` gives us the oldest pending transfer to process next. The `peek` operation lets you look at the front element without removing it, like `Transfer front = pendingTransfers.peek()` to check which request is next without pulling it out. The `isEmpty` operation tells you if the line is empty, as in `if (pendingTransfers.isEmpty())` so you know there is no work left.

In Java, the `Queue` interface is implemented by `LinkedList` and `ArrayDeque`. For example, `Queue<String> line = new LinkedList<>();` creates a queue and `line.offer("SAV2001")` adds to the rear while `line.poll()` removes from the front. The `offer` and `poll` methods are preferred over `add` and `remove` because they return a safe value instead of throwing an exception when the queue is full or empty.

A senior-level nuance is that queues are the backbone of asynchronous systems. Message brokers like Kafka and RabbitMQ are distributed queues. When a bank processes millions of transactions, it enqueues them and worker threads dequeue and process them one by one, which smooths out traffic spikes and keeps the system fair and ordered.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, fund transfer requests arrive all day long. During salary day, thousands of requests arrive in a few minutes. If the bank tries to process all of them at the exact same moment, the system crashes. The bank needs to line them up and process them one at a time, in the order they arrived, so that the customer who clicked first is processed first. This is exactly how a queue works — requests join at the back and are served from the front in fair order.

Problem 2 — Rajesh submits a transfer at 9:00:01 AM and Priya submits one at 9:00:02 AM. It would be unfair if Priya's request got processed before Rajesh's just because of random thread timing. A queue guarantees the order, so Rajesh is always served before Priya.

In our mini-project we build a `TransferQueueProcessor`. It holds pending `TransferRequest` objects in a queue. The `submitTransfer` method enqueues a request. The `processNext` method dequeues the oldest request and processes it. We will enqueue three requests and process them in order, proving FIFO behavior.

The code will contain a `TransferRequest` class holding the from account, to account, and amount. It will contain a `TransferQueueProcessor` class that wraps a `Queue`. The main demo will submit Rajesh's, Priya's, and a third request, then process them one by one and log the FIFO order.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: three transfer requests submitted in this order — Rajesh to Priya Rs.50000, then Priya to Rajesh Rs.12000, then Rajesh to Priya Rs.3000.

Step 1: We call `submitTransfer` with the Rs.50000 request. The `offer` method places it at the rear. The queue now holds exactly one element at the front.

Step 2: We call `submitTransfer` with the Rs.12000 request. It joins behind the first one. The queue now has two elements; the Rs.50000 request is still at the front.

Step 3: We call `submitTransfer` with the Rs.3000 request. It joins at the very back. The queue holds three elements in order: Rs.50000, Rs.12000, Rs.3000.

Step 4: We call `processNext`. The `poll` method removes the front element, which is the Rs.50000 request, and processes it. The queue now holds two elements.

Step 5: We call `processNext` again. It removes the Rs.12000 request. One element remains.

Step 6: We call `processNext` one last time. It removes the Rs.3000 request. The queue is now empty and the loop stops.


```
  Submit order: Rs.50000, then Rs.12000, then Rs.3000
    │
    ▼
  enqueue (offer at REAR)
    │  FRONT [ 50000 ] REAR
    │  FRONT [ 50000 | 12000 ] REAR
    │  FRONT [ 50000 | 12000 | 3000 ] REAR
    ▼
  processNext (poll from FRONT)
    │  remove 50000  → queue: [ 12000 | 3000 ]
    │  remove 12000  → queue: [ 3000 ]
    │  remove 3000   → queue: [ ] empty
    ▼
  Result: processed in the SAME order submitted (FIFO)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A queue is a linear data structure that follows the First In First Out principle. You add elements at the rear using an enqueue operation and remove them from the front using a dequeue operation. This guarantees that the element that has been waiting the longest is always served first, which makes a queue the natural choice whenever fairness and ordering matter.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India, I used a queue to process fund transfer requests. On salary day thousands of requests arrive within minutes, and processing them all at once would overwhelm the system. So I enqueue each incoming request and a pool of worker threads dequeues and processes them one at a time. Because of the First In First Out guarantee, if Rajesh submits his transfer one second before Priya, his request is always processed first. This keeps the system fair and prevents customers from feeling cheated.

In Java I implemented the queue using the Queue interface backed by a LinkedList, and I preferred the offer and poll methods over add and remove because offer and poll return a safe value instead of throwing an exception when the queue is empty or full. For very high scale, the same idea extends to distributed message brokers like Kafka and RabbitMQ, which are essentially durable queues that let the bank smooth out traffic spikes while preserving order.

The key insight I always mention is that a queue is about decoupling the speed of producers from the speed of consumers. The front end can accept requests very fast and drop them into the queue, while the backend processes them steadily at a safe rate. That is why queues are the backbone of almost every asynchronous banking and trading system I have worked on.
